title: Effects of Acoustic Environment Types on Stress Relief in Urban Parks
research_question: To explore the restorative effect of different urban park sound types on mental stress relief, using electrocardiography (ECG) as a physiological health evaluation index.

participants.description: Undergraduate and graduate students (mean age 24 years, male to female ratio 1.2:1) from China, screened for high stress levels (PSS-14 score ≥ 34).
participants.recruitment: Volunteered to participate in an experiment, informed they would be taking a mid-term exam, and screened using PSS-14.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Participants listened to different types of acoustic environments (natural, human activity, mechanical sounds) at seven representative pilot sites within Xiangjiang Park in Harbin City for 5 minutes at each site. Visual factors were controlled by blindfolds.

measures.construct: Root Mean Square of Successive Differences (RMSSD)

mechanisms: Natural sounds (birdsong, leaf sound, purl) have a strong relieving effect on mental pressure, leading to decreased HR and increased RMSSD.
Mechanical sounds (car sound, horn sound, machine sound) have an obvious impediment effect on the recovery of mental pressure, leading to increased HR and decreased RMSSD.
Human voice (conversation, playful sound) has no obvious impediment effect, with mixed effects on HR and RMSSD.
Wind and broadcast sound have little impact on the recovery of mental pressure.
implementation_implications: Future urban park planning and design should clarify acoustic environment functions in different spaces and control dynamic/static rhythms to meet user needs.
Reduce the impact of traffic noise on urban parks by using shrubs and trees as barriers along roadsides.
Introduce more natural sounds, such as flowing water (fountains, waterfalls) to mask unwanted sounds and increase biodiversity to enrich natural sounds.
Create sound environment landscapes to divert attention from negative sounds or use soothing music to mask noise and create local activity atmospheres.
Improve park management and maintenance to reduce behavioral interference with the park sound environment.

limitations: The quantification of park sound environments through subjective questionnaires makes the study subjective.

The standard values of physiological indicators vary from person to person, and the sample size is relatively small, limiting the ability to determine optimal sound proportions for restorative benefits.
The object of study is relatively single (only one park), leading to potential regional limitations.
The acoustic environment involves more than just sound type; environmental temperature and biological diversity may also affect the sound environment.
Testers were all school students (average age 24 years), and the relationship between physiological responses and sound perception may vary across different age groups.
The study was conducted in a single season, not accounting for seasonal factors.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Urban public space environments are critical to the health of residents. In previous studies on urban park environments and health, landscape environment questionnaires have been the main method to evaluate the environmental quality and comfort of urban parks. The research on sound perception also focuses on the exploration of evaluation methods and evaluation indicators; there is little objective empirical evidence in these studies. To further explore the nature of the health role of urban parks, this study started with the sound types of urban parks, based on a field survey, combined the electrocardiogram (ECG) index with the sound type of the park through a portable intelligent device, and HR and RMSSD were selected as the ECG indicators to evaluate the stress relief status. The regression model between the type of acoustic environments and the ECG data was established through the analysis of relevant data. This paper tries to improve the physiological recovery benefit and influence mechanism of sound types in urban parks from an objective point of view and puts forward reasonable suggestions to improve the sound environment in urban parks. The preliminary results show that, in a short time frame, natural sound has a strong relieving effect on mental pressure, while mechanical sound has an obvious impediment effect on the recovery of mental pressure. The results also reveal that the human voice has no obvious impediment effect, and changes in wind and broadcast sound have little impact on the recovery of mental pressure.
